title: 3D multi-material 420 stainless steel-copper parts for improved thermal conductivity of plastic injection moulds: a step forward in laser powder bed fusion
abstract: Abstract The demand for manufacturing multi-functional parts is increasing by the requirement for versatile parts that can adapt to different functions, all in the same component. 3D Multi-Material Laser Powder Bed Fusion is an advanced manufacturing tool to enable the fabrication of complex multi-functional parts. In the present study, this technology was exploited to print multi-material part of high-strength 420 stainless steel alloy with copper heat flow channels, all printed at once. This solution aims to enhance the capacity of plastic injection moulds to extract heat with minimum impact in the mechanical strength. The processing strategy, the interface region between both materials, and the stresses associated with thermal cycles of the plastic injection moulding process are analysed and discussed from a metallurgical, mechanical, and thermal point of view. The 420 stainless steel-copper interface was found to be well-defined and sharp, with no significant diffusion being observed both in the as-built sample and samples subjected to continuous thermal cycles. The incorporation of 4 vol.% copper led to a ~ 22% reduction in the electrical resistivity of the multi-material samples (~ 31 µΩ cm) compared to the mono-material specimens resulting in a thermal conductivity of the 420 stainless steel-copper sample (23.37 W/m K) significantly higher than that of the 420 stainless steel samples (15.30 W/m K). No cracks associated with the continuous heating and cooling steps inherent to the mould were detected, but changes in the microstructure and consequently in the hardness values were observed.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Additive manufacturing has revolutionized the manufacturing industry due to its unique ability to produce geometrically intricate and final functioning components in a single step [ 1 ,  2 ,  3 – 4 ]. Particularly, laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is commonly used in the manufacturing of dense metallic parts since it allows near-net shape production with high accuracy [ 1 ,  5 ,  6 ]. Currently, one of the key areas of research has been mono-material parts with gradual density or microstructure variations due to their simplicity of processing. However, some parts from other industries such as injection moulding, aerospace, biomedical, and automotive must perform in harsh environments. As a result, there is a need for multifunctional parts that can adapt to varied environments, which drives up the demand of producing multi-material parts. [ 3 ,  7 ,  8 – 9 ].

A 3D multi-material part physically combines multiple materials, integrating their properties and functions to achieve customized characteristics in specific areas of the component [ 3 ,  10 ]. The production of these parts by LPBF continues to be a big challenge because it requires a critical understanding of the material properties and prediction of its behaviour, the formation of intermetallic phases, the residual stresses involved in the process, the phase transformations, and the crystallographic defects generated during production [ 3 ,  11 ,  12 ]. These are complex scientific aspects related to the fluid dynamics and thermodynamics of the melt pool, as well as the phase transition and the thermodynamics of the materials themselves [ 3 ]. Additionally, powder stacking and selection of processing parameters namely laser power, scanning speed, layer thickness, hatch spacing, scanning strategy, build orientation, among others, are strongly influenced by the selected materials and their interactions [ 4 ,  13 ,  14 ].

Multi-material solutions could show great potential application in the manufacture of moulds of major importance in the plastic injection moulding industry [ 15 ,  16 ]. One of the biggest challenges in this industry continues to be cooling time and, therefore, several studies have been carried out in this regard, with the aim of making the process more efficient by the integration of advanced cooling channels and different materials [ 8 ,  12 ,  17 ,  18 ,  19 – 20 ]. The production of conformal cooling channels and high thermal conductive inserts (made by copper) is only possible due to the high degree of freedom inherent to the LPBF technology [ 21 ,  22 – 23 ]. Török et al .  [ 22 ] produced a hybrid mould insert by LPBF based on steel and copper, reducing the cooling time by 15%. Mazumder et al .  [ 24 ] fabricated an H13 steel mould insert with a copper heat sink and showed a decrease in the cycle time of 40% compared to a conventional steel mould. Imran et al .  [ 25 ] claimed that a mould produced with steel and copper reduced the cooling time by 30%. Ahn and Kim [ 26 ] created a hybrid mould combining a P21 steel, copper alloy (Ampcoloy 940), and a nickel-copper alloy to maintain high strength and dissipate heat better. Therefore, mould efficiency can be improved with a multi-material approach by combining steel alloys with high thermal conductive materials. However, it is necessary to consider that copper and their alloys are limited in terms of processability and mechanical performance, which can result in premature mould failures.

Although different studies have already been carried out on multi-material solutions produced by additive manufacturing techniques [ 27 ,  28 ,  29 ,  30 – 31 ], several authors have presented difficulties in combining dissimilar materials, such as steel alloys and copper due to the significant differences in their physical and chemical properties, namely melting point, thermal conductivity, specific heat capacity, and expansion coefficient, as well as the composition of the two metals [ 12 ,  30 ,  32 ,  33 ]. These characteristics make it difficult for the two materials to bond well, and to create parts free of defects, cracks or pores after printing. Moreover, there are no intermetallic phases in the Fe–Cu phase diagram, except a very limited amount of solubility between the two elements [ 30 ,  32 ]. Optimized processing parameters with beneficial scanning strategy can be adopted to overcome the abovementioned issues and ensure the structural integrity of the build part, namely the.

The significant difference in terms of thermal conductivity (≅ 25 W/m K to 420 stainless steel [ 34 ] and ≅ 400 W/m K to copper [ 35 ]) can be beneficial for LPBF processing of these materials, as the low thermal conductivity of 420 stainless steel helps retaining heat in the melt pool during copper solidification, resulting in better consolidated layers with fewer pores. Yang et al .  [ 36 ] studied the mechanical and thermal behaviour of the C18150 copper alloy, as well as its densification, and concluded that low laser powers and high scan speeds (low energy densities) lead to worse densification since the energy is not enough to induce the total melt of the powder, leading only to its partial melt. One the other hand, at very high energy densities (high laser powers and low scan speeds), the extremely high cooling rate means that the ambient gas present in the molten pool during the LPBF process does not have enough time to escape, which results in the formation of pores. Jadhav et al .  [ 37 ] studied the densification of pure copper and also concluded that generally, the density of the parts increases with increasing laser power or decreasing scan speed. Therefore, the short cooling time is not enough to fill and close the keyhole with liquid metal. Silbernagel et al .  [ 38 ] stated that it is difficult to produce highly densified copper due to its reflectivity in the infrared region combined with its high thermal conductivity. On the other hand, regarding multi-material production, Liu et al .  [ 39 ] reported the existence of pores and cracks in the processing of 2D multi-material 316L stainless steel-CuSn10 parts due to incompatibility in thermal properties. Cunha et al .  [ 12 ] developed a multi-material solution based on 420 stainless steel and copper with good metallurgical bonding between the two materials, being observed few pores and cracks, but did not quantify the level of densification.

The bond between two metals using the Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) technique is achieved through the localized melting of powders. One of the main challenges in producing multi-material 3D components with LPBF, particularly when different materials are incorporated within the same layer, is ensuring strong metallurgical bonding between adjacent laser tracks while preserving the distinct properties of each material. To address this challenge, it is essential to optimize processing parameters and scanning strategies. These must ensure adequate densification at the interface while minimizing significant diffusion between the materials, thus assuring the structural integrity of the final part.

The present work focuses on the production of a 420 stainless steel-copper part by multi-material LPBF, control of material interactions, diffusion, and phases involved, as well as the material property-processing relationships. The novelty of the solution that is proposed concerns the creation of copper heat flow channels along the structural material (420 stainless steel) in a single production process, with the aim to achieve an engineering solution capable of improving the overall performance of the plastic injection mould, without compromising its integrity. Considering the stresses to which a mould is subjected during its operation, studies related to diffusion, thermal conductivity, and thermal fatigue were carried out.

sections.heading: Powder materials
paragraphs: The 420 stainless steel (420SS) and copper powders were supplied by Carpenter Additive (United Kingdom) and TLS Technik (Germany), with a particle size between 15 and 45 µm, respectively (Fig.  1 ). Their chemical compositions, provided by the suppliers, are shown in Table  1 . Fig. 1 a  420 stainless steel and  b  pure copper (reproduced from [ 17 ,  40 ]) Table 1 Chemical composition of 420SS and copper powder particles (wt.%) Raw material C O Cr Mn N S P Fe Cu 420SS 0.22 0.02 13.5 0.29 0.09 0.004 0.015 Balance – Cu – 0.03 – – – – – – 99.7

The characterisation of the powders was performed elsewhere [ 17 ,  40 ]. Both powders present particles with a spherical shape, the steel alloy powder being composed of martensite (α’) and austenite (γ), and the copper by an fcc structure.

sections.heading: LPBF process and 3D multi-material solution
paragraphs: A 3D multi-material laser powder bed fusion equipment developed at Center for MicroElectroMechanical Systems (CMEMS) in the University of Minho was used to print the 420 stainless steel-Cu parts. This system is constituted of two simultaneous and independent powder deposits (for 420SS and copper powders), two recoaters (used to alternately spread two feedstock materials), and two vacuum cleaning systems (to clean and replace the powder materials). A Bende BD-HZ300W Laser Welding Machine (China) with a Nd: YAG laser with a wavelength of 1064 nm, frequency of 30 Hz, maximum power of 300 W, pulse width between 0.2 and 20 ms, and minimum laser spot diameter of 0.2 mm was used as energy source of the equipment. Moreover, since oxidation is one of the main issues when processing copper alloys with LPBF technology, the 3D multi-material samples were produced in a protective atmosphere (argon) with a gas pressure of 2.5 bar. A schematic representation of the process used as well as the systems involved in the fabrication can be found elsewhere [ 12 ]. Both materials were deposited and processed on an annealed 420 stainless steel build plate which was maintained at a temperature of 150 ºC (thermocouple measured).

The design of the 3D 420 stainless steel-copper multi-material samples consisted of four copper channels surrounded by the steel alloy to avoid contact with the injected material when implemented in a plastic injection mould, preventing premature deterioration of the copper and ensuring the necessary mechanical resistance. A schematic representation of the designed and produced samples is shown in Fig.  2 . The samples produced present a cubic shape with a side length of approximately 3.5 mm and were produced with a bidirectional scan strategy, without rotation between each layer. The processing parameters used for each material are presented in Table  2  and they rely on preliminary optimization studies. The laser power used for copper was higher than for 420 stainless steel powder because the former has significantly higher thermal conductivity, which difficult complete melting. Furthermore, the hatch spacing for copper was also higher to prevent the mixing of powders and the properties of individual materials from being affected. Fig. 2 Design of the 3D 420 stainless steel-copper multi-material samples: sectional view of  a  xy-plane, and  b  xz-plane Table 2 LPBF processing parameters for 420 stainless steel and copper Processing parameters 420 stainless steel Copper Laser power (W) 50 70 Scanning speed (mm/s) 10 10 Layer thickness (µm) 75 75 Hatch spacing (µm) 250 350 Shield gas Argon Laser Beam diameter 200 μm

The LPBF process consisted of two steps (Fig.  3 ). The first step is related to the printing of mono-material layers of 420 stainless steel on the build plate. Twelve single tracks of 420 stainless steel with a length of 3.5 mm and a distance between them of 250 µm were scanned by the laser. After printing of these layers, the second step consisted in printing five multi-material layers. Two single tracks of copper with a length of 2.5 mm were melted and solidified on the previously sintered 420 stainless steel. The remaining previously defined area is filled with 420 stainless steel powder and sintered. After that, steps 1 and 2 were repeated. Finally, twelve new layers of 420 stainless steel were scanned to obtain the final part. Fig. 3 Schematic representation of the design and scan strategies used to build mono- and multi-material layers of 420SS-copper samples

After printing, the samples were polished with SiC abrasive papers down to a 4000 mesh and cleaned ultrasonically in an isopropyl alcohol (IPA) bath for 10 min. Taking as starting point the laser beam diameter and the build envelope, the final samples consisted of 96% of 420 stainless steel and 4% of copper (vol.%) based on the design shown in Figs.  2  and  3 .

sections.heading: Morphological characterisation
paragraphs: Ultra-high-resolution field emission scanning electron microscopy (SEM) (NanoSEM-FEI Nova 200) was used to analyse both the melt pool and polished surfaces (top and cross-section surfaces). The structural and phase analysis of the samples (as-built and after thermal fatigue) was performed by X-ray diffraction (XRD) (PANalytical X’Pert PRO MPD with Co Kα radiation).

The porosity of the as-built samples was determined by mercury intrusion porosimetry (4-33,000 absolute psi) by means of an AutoPore IV, model 9500, Micrometrics apparatus and the findings were compared to those obtained using image analysis software (ImageJ). The width and depth of the melt pool and copper channels were measured using image analysis software as well.

sections.heading: Diffusion
paragraphs: In-service, a plastic injection mould is subject to temperature cycles, which can lead to diffusion and chemical reactions of the materials that constitute it. In this sense, the 420 stainless steel-copper multi-material samples were placed into a furnace (Thermolab supplier), heated to 370 ºC, with a heating rate of 5 ºC/min, maintained at that temperature for 24, 48, and 72 h, and then cooled in air to room temperature. The defined temperature corresponds to the injection temperature of a typical polymeric material [ 41 ,  42 – 43 ].

After each of the thermal cycles, the samples were cut along the xz-plane by using a diamond cutting wheel, polished with SiC abrasive papers down to a 4000 mesh, and cleaned ultrasonically in an isopropyl alcohol bath for 7 min. The 420 stainless steel-copper as-built samples were also included in the analysis as a reference. The morphology of the cross-section of the samples was analysed using SEM and possible changes in chemical composition were evaluated by EDS analysis.

sections.heading: Thermal conductivity
Thermal fatigue assessment
paragraphs: The printed multi-material parts were submitted to thermal fatigue tests in a home-made equipment developed at CMEMS (Fig.  4 ) to replicate a typical plastic injection temperature/time cycle within a mould. The thermal fatigue test is characterized by using external heating and cooling sources that can rapidly heat and cool the samples or localised areas thereof. Fig. 4 Schematic representation of the thermal fatigue test equipment

The thermal fatigue cycle to which the multi-material samples were subjected consisted of three stages (Fig.  5 ). The first stage corresponds to heating of the samples in the furnace up to 370 ºC (thermocouple measurement inside the furnace) for 105 s. Then, the samples were kept inside the furnace for a dwell time of 10 s. After that, the samples were cooled down to 100 ºC (20 s) with a fan. This temperature corresponds to the temperature at which a typical polymeric material can be ejected from the mould without distortion occurring [ 41 ,  42 ]. Fig. 5 Thermal fatigue cycle

Therefore, one entire cycle (heating, dwell time, and cooling) consisted of a total time of 135 s. To evaluate the influence of the number of thermal cycles on the final structure of the samples (2 per condition), five sets were tested (210, 420, 630, 840, and 1050 cycles). A total o X samples After completion of each number of cycles, the samples were sectioned to inspect the occurrence of cracks at the interface between the 420 stainless steel and copper and their mean crack length. Furthermore, assessment of the microhardness of the samples were carried out. The Vickers hardness of the samples was evaluated by means of Shimadzu HMV-2 equipment with a load of 100 gf and a dwell time of 15 s (ISO 6507-1:2023).

sections.heading: Morphological analysis
paragraphs: Figure  6  shows SEM images of the 420 stainless steel-copper multi-material samples (Fig.  6 a), as well as xy- (top view—plane parallel to the copper channels) (Fig.  6 b), xz- (side view—perpendicular plane to the copper channels) (Fig.  6 c), and yz- (Fig.  6 d) planes. Additionally, Figs.  6 e and f show the inner of the samples (sectional view) in both top and cross-section surfaces. From Fig.  6 , the total volume of the 420 stainless steel-copper multi-material samples was approximately 39 mm 3 , with the volume of each copper channel of about 0.39 mm 3 . Therefore, the total volume percentage of copper in the sample is 4%. The porosity of the sample determined by image analysis (ImageJ) based on the top and cross-section surfaces of the multi-material samples was approximately 1.289 ± 0.042%. The mercury intrusion porosimetry revealed a slightly higher porosity of 2.435%, and an average pore diameter of approximately 0.012 µm. Hence, it was concluded that no substantial internal porosity existed in the samples. Fig. 6 420 stainless steel-copper multi-material sample:  a  isometric view,  b  xy-plane (top view),  c  xz-plane (side view),  d  yz-plane,  e  sectional view in xy-plane, and  f  sectional view in xz-plane

The initial attempts to produce 420 stainless steel-copper multi-material parts using LPBF encountered challenges in adequately melting copper, primarily due to its high laser reflectivity, low absorption, and high thermal conductivity. As a result, it became necessary to study the influence of laser power on the melt pool dimensions to achieve full copper melting without compromising the integrity of the interface. As mentioned earlier, the first copper layer was melted over a previously printed, uniform layer of 420 stainless steel to improve bonding by taking advantage of the surface roughness of the top layer. Processing copper in its liquid phase over solid-phase 420 stainless steel ensures full contact between the two materials, enhancing their bonding. As similarly reported by Chen et al .  [ 47 ], it be seen from Fig.  6  that there are natural metallurgical bonds and clear fusion boundaries between the 316L and CuSn10 materials.

sections.heading: Melt pool
paragraphs: The instability of the melt pool, caused by the complex interplay of processing parameters in the LPBF process, is a primary factor contributing to defects in manufactured parts. These defects include poor surface finish, porosity, cracks, balling effect, undesirable microstructures, high residual stresses, partially melted powder, and weak bonding between layers. [ 48 ,  49 ,  50 – 51 ]. Several studies have been carried out to understand the dynamics and geometry of the melt pool, and defects which affect the final properties of the parts produced by LPBF [ 12 ,  48 ,  52 ,  53 ,  54 ,  55 – 56 ]. In this context, various techniques have been employed to study the physical processes associated with the melt pool, including its dynamics, temperature distribution, and spattering, all of which occur during the LPBF process (Fig.  7 a) [ 57 ]. Fig. 7 Melt pool and surface morphology:  a  schematic representation of the physical phenomena associated,  b  isometric view, and  c  top surface

Multiple tracks of 420 stainless steel and copper are represented in Figs.  7 b and c. Both materials presented uniform and consistent melt tracks without any surface pores and directional solidification resultant from the high heat gradient caused by the Nd: YAG laser. No balling effect was observed in the laser tracks indicating that the processing parameters used were appropriate for producing a continuous melt pool for both materials. By Fig.  7 , it is possible to state that the roughness of the copper tracks is significantly higher when compared to the ones of the 420 stainless steel. Ball-shaped asperities can be observed on the boundaries of the copper track (Fig.  6 c) and may occur due to incomplete melting of the powders or spatter effect. Although the copper tracks exhibited some irregularities in the melt pool, the processing conditions were deemed suitable, as there was no indication that these defects affected the solidification or densification of the powders.

sections.heading: Top and cross-section surfaces
paragraphs: The overlap rate between successive tracks of different materials is crucial, as it determines the quality of bonding between them, which in turn influences the densification and surface roughness of LPBF samples. [ 58 ,  59 ]. After some series of preliminary tests, a hatch spacing value of 350 µm was defined for the 420 stainless steel-copper bond. Higher values resulted in some pores and discontinuities in the interface region, while lower values led to a greater mixture of powders in this region, compromising the individuality of the two materials. Furthermore, in the latter case, the width of the copper channels would be smaller, which would make it difficult to quantify their impact on the final multi-material 420 stainless steel-copper sample.

Figure  8  shows SEM images of the top and cross-section surfaces of the 420 stainless steel-copper multi-material samples produced by LPBF. The process begins with mono-material layers of 420 stainless steel and after twelve layers the printing of multi-material layers starts (along five layers). The first deposited copper layer exhibits better densification and consequently lower porosity compared to subsequent layers, due to the concentrated heat retained in the melt pool by the previously sintered 420 stainless steel. The following multi-material layers are already sintered over copper (higher thermal conductivity than steel alloy) and therefore have a higher solidification rate, which makes it more difficult for the copper powder to completely melt. It is possible to claim that the 420 stainless steel and copper regions are almost free of pores, as is the interface between them. It is possible that the gas trapped during the printing process or a lack of fusion is the reason for the small number of visible circular-shaped pores in copper. As a consequence of layer-by-layer processing, the side interfaces (right and left) of the copper channels are not as well defined when compared to the top and bottom of them (Fig.  8 b). Moreover, some cracks, with a few tens of micrometres in size (average size between 10 and 50 µm), were observed, being mostly located at the interface between the two materials and in the central area of the cross-section surface (between copper channels of the same layer). As mentioned in the literature [ 12 ,  30 ,  31 ,  60 ], this phenomenon can occur due to several reasons. It is important to note that 420 stainless steel has low thermal conductivity and, in addition, in the central area of the sample, the steel alloy is less exposed to the surrounding atmosphere, meaning it accumulates more heat than the side zones. Moreover, copper, due to its high thermal conductivity, has an easier heat flow. As a result, the central area of the sample experiences the highest thermal gradient during the process, leading to the development of stresses and, consequently, the formation of cracks (Fig.  8 b—Zone 2). Besides, some cracks might be due to local excessive (non-equilibrium) stresses. Because of the two materials’ differing thermal conductivity and thermal expansion coefficients, temperature gradients that surpass the local strength at certain locations during cooling may cause cracks. [ 12 ,  30 ,  32 ,  33 ]. This discrepancy in values may result in considerable deformations and residual stresses at the interface between the 420 stainless steel and copper. Fig. 8 420 stainless steel-copper multi-material samples:  a  top (sectional view of xy-plane), and  b  cross-section surfaces (sectional view of xz plane)

The width of the copper channel was measured in the top and cross-section surfaces and revealed an average value of about 369.2 ± 6.3 µm. On the other hand, the height of the copper channel was approximately 440.0 ± 11.6 µm.

sections.heading: Thermal behaviour
paragraphs: In plastic injection moulding, the response of materials to temperature and their thermal characteristics, particularly thermal conductivity, are critical factors. While it is well established that cooling time remains one of the significant challenges in this industry, it is also important to recognize that the mould is subjected to temperature cycles during operation. These cycles can induce reactions and alterations in the metallographic structure of the materials. The morphologies and EDS mapping of the 420 stainless steel-copper multi-material samples are shown in Fig.  9 . EDS analysis was performed in two different regions of the samples’ cross-section surface, marked as Zone 1 and Zone 2. Fig. 9 Surface morphology and EDS mapping of the cross-section surface interface of the 420 stainless steel-copper (elements of zone 1 and zone 2 marked by solid and dashed lines, respectively)

As mentioned previously, the top and bottom (perpendicular to the building direction) of the copper channels present a well-defined interface while the side interfaces (parallel to the build direction) reveal some vagueness in certain regions due to the mixing of powders that takes place during the LPBF process. The EDS analysis of Zone 1 (solid line) showed that, as expected by the Fe–Cu phase diagram, there was no elemental diffusion between the main elements of steel alloy and copper. The EDS map of Zone 2 (dashed line) revealed that in the areas relating to each individual material, there is some percentage, albeit residual, of the other constituent, due to the placement of different powders in the same layer and eventually incomplete aspiration between the deposition of each of the materials. The observation made in Zone 2 are aligned with the EDS profile of the 316L/CuSn10 multi-material parts reported by Chen et al .  [ 47 ]. Additionally, similar chemical composition results were reported for 316L-CuCrZr multi-material parts studied by Martendal et al .  [ 61 ].

sections.heading: Diffusion analysis
paragraphs: Considering the aspects mentioned above, diffusion between the two materials would not be expected during the mould operation. Despite this, the samples were heated at 370 ºC for 24, 48, and 72 h and after this time their morphology and chemical composition were compared with the as-built sample (Fig.  10 ). Even for the longest dwell time (72 h), the interface region between the steel (iron) and copper continues to be narrow (around 5 µm), with an abrupt Fe–Cu transition. As observed for the as-built samples, small oscillations in the areas corresponding to each individual material were observed, indicating the presence of residual powder from the previous material during the printing of the subsequent material. Fig. 10 Elements maps of the interface between steel alloy and copper of:  a  as-built sample (reference), and samples heated at 370 ºC for  b  24 h,  c  48 h, and  d  72 h

sections.heading: Thermal conductivity
paragraphs: The values of the electrical resistivity and thermal conductivity of the mono- and multi-material samples are presented in Fig.  11 . Fig. 11 Calculated electrical resistivity and thermal conductivity of 420 stainless steel and 420 stainless steel-copper samples

The electrical resistivity of the mono-material sample (39.75 µΩ cm) is in accordance with the values reported in the literature for this 420 stainless steel [ 62 ,  63 ]. The addition of 4 vol.% of copper resulted in a decrease (≅ 22%) in the electrical resistivity value of the multi-material (31.12 µΩ cm) when compared to the mono-material sample. Consequently, the resulting thermal conductivity of the 420 stainless steel-copper sample (23.37 W/m K) was substantially higher than the one of the 420 stainless steel sample (15.30 W/m K). This means that adding a small amount of copper leads to an improvement in thermal conductivity by 1.5 times due to the abrupt difference between the thermal conductivity of the two materials. These results are similar to those reported by Imran et al .  [ 25 ]. Considering the rule of mixtures, a thermal conductivity value of approximately 39.90 W/m K was obtained for the 420 stainless steel-copper multi-material sample. This is a crude model that ignores interface features and defects. [ 8 ,  17 ,  64 ,  65 ]. In fact, it is known that the level of densification and defects at the interface, namely pores and cracks, play an important role in the thermal properties of the samples [ 66 ]. This explain why the value obtained experimentally was slightly lower than the one calculated by the rule of mixtures.

Török et al .  [ 22 ] produced a hybrid mould insert by LPBF based on steel and copper, reducing the cooling time by 15%. Mazumder et al .  [ 24 ] fabricated an H13 steel mould insert with a copper heat sink and showed a decrease in the cycle time of 40% compared to a conventional steel mould. Imran et al .  [ 25 ] claimed that a mould produced with steel and copper reduced the cooling time by 30%.

Although steel-copper-based structures have recently garnered attention due to their unique properties, there have been limited studies on their thermal properties, and most of these studies rely on theoretical calculations. Recently, Cunha et al .  [ 8 ,  17 ] developed two studies combining 420 stainless steel and copper by hot pressing and determined the thermal conductivity of the solutions developed. The measured values were higher than those obtained in the current study. This discrepancy may be attributed to the higher copper content in the previous study and the lower number of pores, which can reduce the thermal properties.

sections.heading: Thermal fatigue
paragraphs: A plastic injection mould experiences a complex combination of high mechanical and thermal stresses during the injection process. Thermal fatigue is a known phenomenon that can occur with or without mechanical loads [ 67 ]. Therefore, thermal fatigue is an important characteristic that can shorten the useful life of the mould and reduce the reliability of the material [ 68 ,  69 ,  70 – 71 ]. Typically, the thermal fatigue behaviour of these tools depends mainly on the thermal expansion coefficient and high-temperature strength of the mould materials [ 72 ]. This is characterised by the existence of micro- or macroscopic cracks resulting from cyclic thermal stresses and strains, as occurs in successive cycles of the injection moulding process, due to temperature changes, temperature gradients, and high temperatures under constrained thermal deformation.

As previously shown, the as-built multi-material 420 stainless steel-copper samples exhibited a well-defined interface between the two materials, characterized by the absence of pores, diffusion, and significant cracks. However, occasional crack arrest regions were observed at the interface between the two materials (Fig.  12 ). Although the occurrence of these regions is still not well understood, the existence of defects, namely lack of fusion or gas trapped, at the interface between materials may be at their origin. Furthermore, and particularly the production of multi-material parts based on steel and copper, leads to the formation of microstructures with very different particle sizes (due to the inherent properties of each material), which can contribute to the formation of crack arrest at their interface [ 73 ,  74 – 75 ]. Moran et al .  [ 74 ] state that crack arrest has a significant impact on the fatigue of metals produced by Additive Manufacturing. Fig. 12 SEM images of the interface 420 stainless steel copper where zone 1 represents a suitable metallurgical bonding between the two materials, and zone 2 shows a crack arrest region in the interface

The number of cracks per millimetre, mean crack length, maximum crack length, and crack density are some of the parameters evaluated when analysing the thermal fatigue behaviour of materials. In this sense, and in order to compare with the results obtained for the as-built samples, the occurrence of cracks in the interface between 420 stainless steel and copper and the mean length of the existing cracks were evaluated. The first case is essential to evaluate since, as the two materials have different thermal expansion coefficient values (10.8 × 10 –6  K −1  for 420 stainless steel [ 76 ] and 19.2 × 10 –6  K −1  for copper [ 77 ] at a temperature of 370 ºC), they can expand/contract too much, leading to the rupture of the bonding and consequently the creation of cracks. Conversely, evaluating the mean crack length is important because cracks inherent to the LPBF process were already present (Fig.  8 b). It is crucial to determine whether these cracks grew during the thermal cycles. Figure  13  shows the interface of the 420 stainless steel-copper multi-material samples subjected to 210, 420, 630, 840, and 1050 cycles of heating and cooling. Fig. 13 The interface of the 420 stainless steel-copper multi-material samples after thermal fatigue tests

As mentioned previously, cracks inherent to the process were observed in the central zone of the samples produced by LPBF (between the copper channels of the same layer). Figure  14  shows the mean crack length for different thermal fatigue test times. The multi-material sample in the as-built condition is also included as a reference. Fig. 14 Mean crack length for different thermal fatigue test times

By Fig.  14 , it is possible to state that the mean crack length is within the same range of values for any of the conditions. Furthermore, there was no marked trend in the crack length with the increase in the number of cycles of the thermal fatigue test. In other words, as the differences observed in relation to the as-built condition are too small, considering the range of values and standard deviations presented, it is thought that these are associated with the process itself, that is, the samples used in each of the tests do not have the same cracks with the same lengths, hence the differences observed.

Figure  15  presents the XRD patterns of the 420 stainless steel-copper samples in the as-built condition and after 630 and 1050 thermal fatigue cycles (up to 370 ºC). The as-built part comprised martensite, residual austenite, and copper. With an increasing number of thermal fatigue cycles, a decrease in the intensity of the residual austenite peak was observed. It is known that this phase tends to transform to α-Fe + Fe 3 C in the temperature range of the thermal fatigue tests carried out (tempering). Also, the martensite lose carbon transforming to the same equilibrium phases, leading to a hardness decrease. To confirm these phase transformations, microhardness values were carried out on the base material (steel) of samples subject to thermal fatigue. The values are presented in Fig.  16  and confirm the XRD analysis. The hardness of the 420 stainless steel decreased with the increase in the number of thermal fatigue cycles, although the greatest variation was observed just after 210 cycles. The hardness values tended to stabilise after 420 cycles. The thermal fatigue cycles did not influence the hardness of the copper (79.8 ± 6.3 HV for the control sample and 77.0 ± 6.4 HV after 1050 cycles). sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: This study consisted of the production of a multi-material design solution for plastic injection moulds, consisting of the incorporation of copper cooling channels in a 420 stainless steel part by Laser Powder Bed Fusion. The following conclusions may be drawn: Multi-material 420 stainless steel-copper samples, with a 4% copper volume fraction and an overall densification of 96%, were successfully produced. The morphological analysis indicated a low number of pores and cracks in both the individual materials and their interface. The pores observed in the copper were circular in shape, while cracks measuring a few tens of micrometers in size were detected in the interface zone. This region is well-defined and features a thin diffusion zone. The samples subjected to plastic injection temperature (370 ºC) during 24, 48, and 72 h also revealed a narrow interface region without diffusion maintaining an abrupt Fe-Cu transition. The thermal properties of the multi-material 420 stainless steel-copper were improved by 1.5 times without compromising the mechanical strength of the 420 stainless steel. No cracks associated with the continuous heating and cooling steps (thermal fatigue cycles) inherent to the mould and the plastic injection moulding process were detected. At the microstructural level, XRD analysis revealed a decrease in the intensity of the residual austenite peak with the increase in the number of thermal fatigue cycles, due to the austenite transformation into α-Fe + Fe 3 C. This led to a hardness decrease of the steel.
